detail.what_it_is: A candlestick where the open and close prices are approximately equal, producing a very small body. Body <= 10% of the candle's full range (high to low). Signal: market indecision -- buyers and sellers pushed in opposite directions but price returned close to where it opened.

types.name: Gravestone Doji
types.description: Long upper wick, open/close near the low -- more bearish bias within the indecision signal.

why_location_matters.principle: A Doji's meaning depends entirely on WHERE it forms.

cases.meaning: Possible sign price is pausing before a bullish move -- requires confirmation.

detail.what_it_is: A candle with a small body positioned in the LOWER portion of its range, an upper wick at least 2x the body length, and a minimal or absent lower wick. Signal strength is generally considered WEAKER than a standard Hammer -- Hammer's long lower wick shows buying pressure was absorbed and held; Inverted Hammer's long upper wick shows buying pressure was attempted and REJECTED, which is a less committed signal of exhaustion even though it still points the same direction.

types.name: Hanging Man
types.description: Hammer's exact shape, uptrend-into-resistance context instead of downtrend-into-support -- read as a bearish reversal warning instead of a bullish reversal signal.

detail.distinction_from_hammer: This is the single most important thing to understand about Hanging Man: it is the SAME candle shape as Hammer, pixel for pixel. The ONLY difference is trend context -- Hammer forms after a downtrend at support (bullish read); Hanging Man forms after an uptrend at resistance (bearish read). Because the shapes are visually identical, context is not a nice-to-have filter here the way it sometimes reads for other patterns -- it is the ENTIRE basis for which signal (if any) the candle actually means. A trader who reads candle shape alone, without checking trend context, cannot tell a Hammer from a Hanging Man at all.

why_location_matters.principle: Occurring at a resistance zone after a genuine uptrend strengthens the bearish reversal read, same principle used throughout this library.

detail.why_self_confirming: Doji and Hammer show INDECISION or a REJECTION WICK on one candle -- by themselves they don't prove which side actually won, so a third candle is needed to confirm direction. Bullish Engulfing is different: the second candle's size and direction ARE the proof. A green candle large enough to fully swallow the prior red candle's body has already demonstrated buyers overwhelmed sellers within that same candle -- there is nothing left for a third candle to confirm that the pattern itself hasn't already shown.

detail.what_it_is: Three consecutive long bullish (green) candles, each closing higher than the previous, each opening within or near the prior candle's body (not gapping wildly away from it), with relatively small wicks on each -- together signaling strong, sustained buying momentum across three full sessions rather than a single reaction candle.

types.name: Three White Soldiers

detail.pattern_type_distinction: Unlike almost every other pattern in this library (Doji, Hammer, Engulfing, Morning Star -- all reversal signals), Three White Soldiers is a trend-CONTINUATION signal, not a reversal pattern. This changes the appropriate location context: it works best breaking out of a consolidation/range or early in a fresh uptrend, NOT at a support level the way reversal patterns need to be. Stated explicitly here since applying reversal-pattern location logic ('near support') to a continuation pattern would be a category error.

why_location_matters.principle: Most effective breaking out of consolidation or early in a new uptrend; a nuance worth flagging explicitly: occurring LATE in an already-extended move can mean the opposite of what it looks like -- exhaustion (a blow-off top) rather than fresh momentum, since three strong candles after a move that has already run far can just as easily be the last gasp of buyers as the start of something new.

cases.location: Breaking out of consolidation/range, or early in a new uptrend
cases.meaning: The classic valid context -- fresh momentum confirming a genuine breakout.

Weaker, and potentially the OPPOSITE signal -- may indicate exhaustion rather than continuation. Flagged as a real nuance, not a hard rule this entry enforces (see thresholds below on why no filter for this was built).

detail.what_it_is: Price levels where the market has previously reversed or paused, acting as psychological/structural barriers to further movement. Support is a 'floor' -- a level where buying pressure has previously stepped in and pushed price back up. Resistance is a 'ceiling' -- a level where selling pressure has previously stepped in and pushed price back down. This is the foundational structural concept nearly every other pattern in this library (Doji, Hammer, Shooting Star, Engulfing, Morning/Evening Star, Liquidity Sweep) depends on for its own 'location' requirement.

types.name: Support
types.description: A price floor -- buyers have previously defended this level, and are expected to again.

types.name: Resistance
types.description: A price ceiling -- sellers have previously defended this level, and are expected to again.

types.name: Role Reversal (support <-> resistance)
types.description: Once a support level is genuinely broken (price closes clearly below it), it can flip and act as NEW resistance on a later retest from below -- and the mirror is true for a broken resistance becoming new support. This is represented in the engine already: support_resistance() recomputes both values continuously from the same underlying swing points, so once price structure shifts, the nearest support/resistance values shift with it -- there is no separate 'this used to be support' flag, the role reversal falls out naturally from always reading the CURRENT nearest levels rather than a fixed historical one.

detail.why_it_matters: A level is not inherently significant just because price is near a round number -- it matters because of MARKET MEMORY: traders who bought/sold there before, and the stop-loss/breakout orders resting around that price, make the market genuinely more likely to react there again. The more times a level has been touched and reacted to, the more traders are watching it, and the more significant it becomes (see risk_note below on what happens after many touches).
detail.how_identified: Mechanically: swing highs and swing lows -- points where price reversed direction for at least one full swing (the same swing-point detection already used throughout this project's strategies, via concepts.swing_points()/concepts.support_resistance()). A swing low that price reversed from becomes a candidate support level; a swing high becomes a candidate resistance level. No separate new detection primitive was built for this entry -- it reuses the existing mechanism strategy-for-strategy, exactly as the task for this entry required.

how_used_in_a_full_setup.principle: Support/Resistance on its own is only half a setup -- it is the LOCATION component that every reaction/confirmation pattern in this library is combined with. None of Doji, Hammer, Shooting Star, Engulfing, or Morning/Evening Star are traded in isolation; each requires 'at support' or 'at resistance' as step 1 before the candle pattern itself even matters (see each entry's own golden_rule).

worked_example.title: Identify the level
worked_example.text: A swing low is confirmed at some price -- this becomes the active support level.

worked_example.title: Price returns to the level
worked_example.text: Later, price moves back down toward that same support level.

worked_example.title: A reaction/confirmation pattern forms there
worked_example.text: E.g. a Hammer forms at the level, followed by a confirmation candle closing above the Hammer's high -- see the Hammer entry for the full sequence.

worked_example.title: Entry, Stop Loss, Take Profit
worked_example.text: Exactly as described in that pattern's own entry -- Support & Resistance supplies the WHERE, the candle pattern supplies the WHEN.

thresholds.value: What counts as a 'touch' or 'reaction' at a level
thresholds.note: Builder's own default, since it isn't fixed elsewhere in this library: a touch is the swing-point mechanism itself registering a reversal at (or very near) the level's price -- price wicking through and closing back on the same side it approached from, using the same swing_points()/support_resistance() logic already shared across every strategy, not a separate new counting rule.

Uses the engine's existing swing_points() default lookback (2 bars either side) unless a specific strategy overrides it -- unchanged from how every prior strategy in this project already reads these two functions.

detail.risk_note: A level that has been tested multiple times is more likely to eventually break -- each touch consumes some of the resting orders that made the level significant in the first place, so a level's defenders get thinner with every successful test. This is the same 'once-tested' logic already used as a hard trading rule in the Dumb Money Concepts strategies (each specific level triggers only ONE trade, ever, then is retired) -- Support & Resistance's own risk profile is the reasoning that rule is built on, made explicit here.
detail.engine_note: This is a display/reference task only. Support/resistance detection itself (concepts.support_resistance(), concepts.swing_points()) is already deeply wired into the backtest engine and reused by nearly every strategy built this session -- this entry documents the concept, it does not add a new one.

detail.what_it_is: Price moves beyond an obvious liquidity area (a previous high/low, equal highs/lows, or a range extreme) -- triggering the stop-losses and breakout orders resting there -- then reverses and closes back on the other side of that level. The critical distinction: a sweep WITHOUT reclaim is a genuine breakout/continuation, not a signal; a sweep WITH reclaim (the reclaim strictly AFTER the sweep) is the valid reversal setup.

types.name: Sweep of a low (bullish setup)
types.description: Price dips below an important low, triggering resting sell-stops, then reclaims back above it.

types.name: Sweep of a high (bearish setup)
types.description: Price spikes above an important high, triggering resting buy-stops, then reclaims back below it.

types.name: Sweep without reclaim (NOT a signal)
types.description: Price moves beyond the level and stays there -- this is a genuine breakout/continuation, the opposite of a reversal signal. See the risk note below.

why_location_matters.principle: A sweep only matters at genuinely important liquidity levels -- ones with real resting orders behind them.

cases.location: Previous swing high/low, equal highs/lows, or a well-defined range extreme
cases.meaning: The classic valid context -- these are exactly where stop-losses and breakout orders cluster.

cases.location: An arbitrary price level with no prior structure
cases.meaning: Weak/low-value -- there's no real liquidity resting there for the 'sweep' to trigger, so a bounce there is much less meaningful.

detail.golden_rule: Important level + Sweep beyond it + Reclaim (sequence-ordered, strictly after the sweep) = valid setup. A sweep alone, without the reclaim, is noise -- often the start of a real breakout, not a reversal.

long_setup.title: Identify the level
long_setup.text: Find an important low (previous low, equal-lows, or range low).

long_setup.title: Sweep
long_setup.text: Price moves below that low, triggering the resting sell-stops there.

long_setup.title: Wait, do not enter yet
long_setup.text: The sweep itself is not the entry signal -- see the risk note on sweep-without-reclaim.

long_setup.title: Reclaim (sequence-ordered)
long_setup.text: Price closes back above the swept low, strictly AFTER the sweep (uses the engine's existing sequential-event/sequence-ordering capability).

long_setup.title: Entry
long_setup.text: At the close of the reclaim candle.

long_setup.title: Stop Loss
long_setup.text: Placed just below the swept low (buffer-verified via cost_model.check_buffer_safety() -- note that this pattern's typical sweep distance beyond the level can itself already exceed the safety threshold, so the buffer check matters more here than on a plain candlestick pattern).

long_setup.title: Take Profit
long_setup.text: At the nearest opposing structure level.

short_setup.title: Stop Loss
short_setup.text: Placed just above the swept high, buffer-verified.

short_setup.title: Take Profit
short_setup.text: At the nearest opposing support level.

detail.risk_note: The single most important distinction for this pattern: a sweep WITHOUT reclaim is not noise to be filtered out incidentally -- it is actively the OPPOSITE case, a genuine breakout/continuation. Entering on the sweep alone, before the sequence-ordered reclaim confirms, risks entering directly against a real breakout in progress. The reclaim is not optional confirmation the way it is for Doji -- for this pattern specifically, no reclaim means no trade, full stop.

Determined dynamically via cost_model.check_buffer_safety(), not a fixed guess -- flagged as especially important for this pattern since the sweep distance itself can already be sizeable.

detail.what_it_is: Two or more swing highs (or lows) at approximately the same price level -- a sign that stop-losses and breakout orders are clustered right at that exact price, making it a concentrated liquidity pool rather than an ordinary single level.

types.name: Equal Highs (EQH)
types.description: Two+ swing highs at nearly the same level -- a resistance-side liquidity pool, often swept before a bearish move.

types.name: Equal Lows (EQL)
types.description: Two+ swing lows at nearly the same level -- a support-side liquidity pool, often swept before a bullish move.

why_location_matters.principle: EQH/EQL near a higher-timeframe level is a stronger liquidity target than an isolated equal pair sitting in open space -- the same 'does this converge with something else important' principle used throughout this library.

cases.meaning: Strong -- multiple reasons for a real reaction converge.
Weaker -- still a real liquidity pool, but with less backing it.

detail.golden_rule: This directly reuses the already-documented Liquidity Sweep concept rather than re-explaining sweep mechanics from scratch: Equal Highs/Lows + a sweep of that level + a reclaim back inside (sequence-ordered, strictly after the sweep) = valid reversal setup. Equal Highs/Lows only supplies WHERE the sweep matters most (a level with real resting orders behind it); the sweep-then-reclaim mechanics themselves are identical to the Liquidity Sweep entry.

detail.what_it_is: The high and low of the previous session/day/week, treated as a significant reference level purely because so many market participants are watching that exact price -- unlike a swing point (whose importance comes from where price itself reversed), a Previous High/Low's importance comes from being a well-known, widely-watched calendar boundary.

types.name: Previous Day High/Low (PDH/PDL)
types.description: Yesterday's (UTC calendar day) high and low -- already computed by the engine's own concepts.previous_day_high_low().

types.name: Previous Week High/Low
types.description: The same underlying concept at a wider time granularity -- last week's high/low instead of yesterday's. Not separately implemented in the engine today; would reuse the exact same weekly-groupby shape previous_day_high_low() already uses for days, if a strategy needed it.

detail.why_it_matters: Unlike the other location-based concepts in this library, Previous High/Low's importance is NOT really about sub-location (there's no 'near support vs in open space' variant here) -- it's that these exact price levels are among the most-watched in the entire market, purely because of what they ARE (yesterday's extremes), not because of anything else nearby. This is a genuine structural difference from Support & Resistance, Order Block, FVG, and Equal Highs/Lows, all of which the significance depends on. Noted explicitly here rather than forcing a 'why location matters' table that wouldn't really apply.
detail.golden_rule: Same discipline as every other concept here: Previous High/Low + a reaction (wick, reclaim) or sweep pattern = valid setup. An isolated touch of PDH/PDL with no reaction is not a signal by itself.

long_setup.text: The previous session's low (concepts.previous_day_high_low()'s PDL -- already causal: yesterday is fully closed by the time today reads it).

Flagged precisely: no existing function combines 'day-boundary level' with 'sequence-ordered reclaim' yet -- a future strategy build would need a small new composition following this exact established pattern, not a new capability.

detail.what_it_is: A three-candle imbalance: an area on the chart where price moved so fast that a gap exists between candle 1's wick and candle 3's wick (candle 2 is the large, fast-moving candle that creates the imbalance). Represents a zone that traded through inefficiently -- no real two-sided (buyer vs seller) battle happened there, just one side sweeping through.

types.name: Bullish FVG
types.description: Formed during an upward move (candle 3's low sits above candle 1's high) -- acts as potential support if price retraces back into it.

types.name: Bearish FVG
types.description: Formed during a downward move (candle 3's high sits below candle 1's low) -- acts as potential resistance if price retraces back into it.

why_location_matters.principle: An FVG formed in the direction of the higher-timeframe trend carries more weight than one against it, and a FRESH (never-revisited) gap is stronger than one already partially filled.

cases.location: Aligned with higher-timeframe bias, still fresh
cases.meaning: The classic valid context -- an efficient continuation zone the broader trend is likely to respect.

cases.location: Against the higher-timeframe bias, or already partially filled
cases.meaning: Weaker -- fighting the larger trend, or the gap's 'magnet' effect has already been partly used up.

detail.golden_rule: Location (aligned with higher-timeframe bias) + a fresh FVG + price actually returning to tag the gap = valid setup -- an FVG sitting untouched on the chart, on its own, is not yet a trade signal.

long_setup.title: Identify the gap
long_setup.text: A bullish FVG forms during an upward move, in the direction of the higher-timeframe bias.

long_setup.title: Wait for the retrace
long_setup.text: Price must return into the gap zone strictly AFTER the FVG forms (uses the engine's existing sequential-event/sequence-ordering capability -- the retrace can never be dated before the gap that created it).

long_setup.title: Reaction confirmation
long_setup.text: Entry at the candle that closes back in the direction of the original move after tagging the gap -- not on the tag itself.

long_setup.title: Entry
long_setup.text: At the close of that reaction candle.

long_setup.title: Stop Loss
long_setup.text: Below the gap's low (buffer-verified via cost_model.check_buffer_safety()).

long_setup.title: Take Profit
long_setup.text: At the nearest opposing resistance/structure level (reuses the existing structure-based TP mechanism).

short_setup.title: Identify the gap
short_setup.text: A bearish FVG forms during a downward move, in the direction of the higher-timeframe bias.

short_setup.title: Wait for the retrace
short_setup.text: Price returns into the gap zone, strictly after the FVG forms.

short_setup.title: Reaction confirmation
short_setup.text: Entry at the candle that closes back down after tagging the gap.

short_setup.title: Entry
short_setup.text: At the close of that reaction candle.

short_setup.title: Stop Loss
short_setup.text: Above the gap's high, buffer-verified.

short_setup.title: Take Profit
short_setup.text: At the nearest opposing support/structure level.

detail.risk_note: An FVG by itself, without higher-timeframe alignment and without waiting for a genuine reaction at the retest, is a weak signal -- plenty of gaps get sliced straight through with no reaction at all. The same once-tested-level caution used elsewhere in this library applies here too: a gap that has already been tagged and reacted to once is a weaker target on a second visit.

thresholds.note: This task originally described FVG detection as reusing a candle_body_pct-based 'large candle' threshold from CRT 2.0. Checked directly against the engine: CRT 2.0 actually uses fvg_zone() (built on fair_value_gap()), which is a pure 3-candle WICK-GAP comparison (candle 3's low > candle 1's high, or the mirror) -- there is no separate body-size/percentage threshold anywhere in this definition, and none is needed, because the gap itself (no overlap between candle 1 and candle 3's wicks) already IS the qualifying test. Documented here accurately rather than repeating the inaccurate premise.
Determined dynamically via cost_model.check_buffer_safety(), not a fixed guess.

detail.what_it_is: The last opposing candle before a strong, decisive move in the other direction -- e.g. the last red candle before a strong bullish breakout is the bullish order block. Represents a zone believed to contain concentrated institutional orders left behind right before the market moved away sharply.

types.name: Bullish Order Block
types.description: The last down-candle before a strong up-move -- a potential support zone on retracement.

types.name: Bearish Order Block
types.description: The last up-candle before a strong down-move -- a potential resistance zone on retracement.

why_location_matters.principle: An order block near a higher-timeframe support/resistance level, or near an untested zone (the same 'untested level' idea the Dumb Money Concepts strategies are built around), is considered more significant than one sitting in the middle of an open range.

cases.location: Near a higher-timeframe level or an untested DMC-style zone
cases.meaning: The classic valid context -- multiple reasons for the market to react converge at the same price.

cases.location: In open space, no nearby structure
cases.meaning: Weaker -- the order block is the only reason for a reaction, with nothing else backing it up.

detail.golden_rule: Location + a genuine order block (confirmed by the strength of the move that followed it) + price returning to retest the block = valid setup.

long_setup.title: Identify the order block
long_setup.text: The last bearish candle before a strong bullish move -- 'strong' is confirmed the same way the engine already confirms it: a genuine Break of Structure (a close beyond the most recent swing high), not a separately guessed size threshold.

long_setup.title: Mark the zone
long_setup.text: That candle's own high-to-low range becomes the order block zone.

long_setup.title: Wait for the retrace
long_setup.text: Price retraces back into the zone, strictly AFTER the initial move (sequence-ordered).

long_setup.title: Reaction confirmation
long_setup.text: Entry at the candle confirming a bounce/reaction within the zone.

long_setup.title: Stop Loss
long_setup.text: Below the order block's low (buffer-verified via cost_model.check_buffer_safety()).

long_setup.title: Take Profit
long_setup.text: At the nearest opposing resistance/structure level.

short_setup.title: Identify the order block
short_setup.text: The last bullish candle before a strong bearish move, confirmed by a Break of Structure down.

short_setup.title: Mark the zone
short_setup.text: That candle's own high-to-low range becomes the order block zone.

short_setup.title: Wait for the retrace
short_setup.text: Price retraces back into the zone, strictly after the initial move.

short_setup.title: Reaction confirmation
short_setup.text: Entry at the candle confirming a rejection within the zone.

short_setup.title: Stop Loss
short_setup.text: Above the order block's high, buffer-verified.

short_setup.title: Take Profit
short_setup.text: At the nearest opposing support/structure level.

detail.risk_note: An order block that has already been tested and reacted to once is weaker on a second test -- the exact 'once-tested' logic already used as a hard trading rule in the Dumb Money Concepts strategies (each specific level triggers only ONE trade, ever). The same caution applies here even though it isn't enforced as a hard filter for this reference entry.

concepts.name: Market Structure Shift (MSS) / Change of Character (CHoCH)

detail.what_it_is: The first structural break of a prevailing trend: in a downtrend (lower highs, lower lows), the first time price closes above a prior swing high signals a potential shift to bullish structure (and the mirror for uptrends breaking down). The engine actually has TWO related implementations of this idea, at two different rigor levels, both reused here rather than building anything new: change_of_character() (a swing-point BOS in the opposite direction of the last BOS -- the existing 'choch' concept, used live by the Double Confirmation CHoCH with Liquidity Trap strategy) and the stricter valid_structure_trend() / valid_structure_trend_soft() (a genuinely stateful 'valid break' machine -- a low only counts once price has closed above the high that predates it -- used live by CRT 2.0 and Liquidity Sweep Reversal). Both represent the same underlying idea; valid_structure_trend() is the more rigorous of the two.

types.name: Bullish CHoCH
types.description: A downtrend's structure breaking to the upside -- the first sign of a potential reversal.

types.name: Bearish CHoCH
types.description: An uptrend's structure breaking to the downside.

types.name: BOS vs CHoCH -- the distinction that matters
types.description: Break of Structure (BOS) is a break that CONTINUES the already-established trend (e.g. a higher high in an uptrend). CHoCH is the FIRST break that goes AGAINST the established trend, signaling a potential reversal. The two are often confused because they use the exact same mechanical test (a close beyond a swing point) -- what differs is only which direction it breaks relative to the CURRENT trend, which is exactly what change_of_character() checks for (a BOS whose direction is opposite the prior BOS's direction).

why_location_matters.principle: A CHoCH occurring at a major higher-timeframe level (support/resistance, or an untested DMC-style level) carries more weight than one occurring in open space, same reasoning as every location-dependent concept in this library.

cases.meaning: The classic valid context -- structure shift AND a level converge.

cases.location: In open space, no nearby level
cases.meaning: Weaker -- more likely to be noise in a ranging market than a genuine reversal.

detail.golden_rule: Location + a genuine structural break confirmed via real swing-detection (not a same-window co-occurrence approximation -- see the risk note below on the sequential_event() fix this session that specifically addressed this exact failure mode) + confirmation retest = valid setup.

long_setup.title: Identify the downtrend
long_setup.text: Lower highs and lower lows, via the engine's existing valid_structure_trend().

long_setup.title: Wait for the break
long_setup.text: Price closes above the most recent lower high -- a genuine CLOSE beyond the prior swing high, not just a wick poking through.

long_setup.title: Optional: wait for a retest
long_setup.text: For extra confirmation, wait for price to retest the broken level (sequence-ordered, strictly after the break) -- this is the RECOMMENDED default entry for this library, consistent with the established preference for confirmed entries over reacting to the break itself.

long_setup.title: Entry -- two options
long_setup.text: Either at the retest reaction (recommended/default) OR at the break candle's own close (faster, less confirmed -- both are flagged here as valid, but the retest version is the default).

long_setup.title: Stop Loss
long_setup.text: Below the most recent swing low, buffer-verified via cost_model.check_buffer_safety().

long_setup.title: Take Profit
long_setup.text: At the nearest resistance/next structural level.

short_setup.title: Identify the uptrend
short_setup.text: Higher highs and higher lows.

short_setup.title: Wait for the break
short_setup.text: Price closes below the most recent higher low.

short_setup.title: Optional: wait for a retest
short_setup.text: Same reasoning as the long side -- the retest version is the recommended default.

short_setup.title: Entry -- two options
short_setup.text: At the retest reaction (recommended) or at the break candle's own close.

short_setup.title: Stop Loss
short_setup.text: Above the most recent swing high, buffer-verified.

short_setup.title: Take Profit
short_setup.text: At the nearest support/next structural level.

detail.risk_note: The primary risk is distinguishing a genuine CHoCH from noise in choppy/ranging conditions -- multiple CHoCH signals firing in a short window without a sustained move afterward should reduce confidence in the level (a descriptive caution, not a hard filter here). This is also exactly the failure mode a real bug fix this session addressed directly: sequential_event()'s ordering check used to be vulnerable to a same-window overlap (an event that satisfies BOTH sides of a two-step sequence on the same bar could silently clobber a genuinely earlier, still-valid reference event) -- confirmed on real Asian Range London Sweep data before the fix, where a legitimate sweep failed to pair with its own reclaim purely because a later bar happened to ALSO look like a fresh sweep. Fixed by checking the second event's condition against state as of the END of the previous bar, before the current bar's own first-event flag can update it -- this is what makes 'genuine structural break, not a same-window approximation' in the golden_rule above an accurate claim rather than an aspirational one.

thresholds.note: This concept reuses 100% existing swing-detection (swing_points()) and sequence-ordering (sequential_event()) infrastructure -- nothing new was built or tuned for this entry.

detail.engine_note: This is a display/reference task only -- both change_of_character() and valid_structure_trend() are already wired into the backtest engine and used live by the Double Confirmation CHoCH with Liquidity Trap, CRT 2.0, and Liquidity Sweep Reversal strategies.

detail.structural_note: IMPORTANT -- this concept works differently from every other entry in this library. It is a LOCATION FILTER for other setups, not a standalone pattern with its own entry/SL/TP. Every section below is reframed accordingly rather than forced into the same template as Doji, FVG, Order Block, etc. -- represented accurately rather than stretched to fit a shape it doesn't have.
detail.what_it_is: Dividing a defined price range (between a significant swing high and swing low) into an upper half ('premium,' where price is relatively expensive, favoring look-for-shorts) and a lower half ('discount,' where price is relatively cheap, favoring look-for-longs). The dividing line (the range's midpoint) is called 'equilibrium.'

types.name: Discount zone
types.description: The lower half of the active range -- price here is 'on sale' relative to the range, the zone that favors looking for LONG entries from another concept.

types.name: Premium zone
types.description: The upper half of the active range -- price here is 'expensive' relative to the range, the zone that favors looking for SHORT entries from another concept.

types.name: Equilibrium (the 50% line itself)
types.description: The exact midpoint dividing premium from discount -- a third reference point worth naming on its own, since price crossing it is itself often watched as a shift in which zone is currently 'active.'

detail.why_location_matters: This concept IS the location-filter -- it doesn't have a separate 'why location matters' the way Order Block or FVG do (those ask 'where is this pattern relative to other structure'; Premium/Discount instead asks 'where in the current range is price right now, and does that support the trade direction'). Explicit design choice: Premium/Discount should be used ALONGSIDE another concept (e.g. only take a long-side Order Block or FVG setup if it also falls in the discount zone of the current range), never traded on its own.
detail.golden_rule: Reframed for this concept, since it doesn't have a standalone golden rule the way other entries do: Premium/Discount zone + another qualifying setup (FVG, Order Block, Liquidity Sweep, a candlestick pattern) occurring within the CORRECT zone for that trade's direction = added confluence. Premium/Discount alone, with no genuine entry trigger from another concept, is never a valid trade by itself.

long_setup.title: Define the active range
long_setup.text: The most recent significant swing high to swing low (concepts.premium_discount_zone() already does this via the engine's existing swing_points()).

long_setup.title: Calculate the discount zone
long_setup.text: The lower 50% of that range is the clean, unambiguous default used here (equilibrium = (swing_high + swing_low) / 2, in_discount = close below equilibrium -- exactly what concepts.premium_discount_zone() already computes and returns). A stricter sub-zone (e.g. only the lower 38-50%, a Fibonacci-style narrowing) is a valid FUTURE refinement, flagged here but not implemented -- 50% is the deliberately simple, already-built default.

long_setup.title: Require it as a filter, not a trigger
long_setup.text: Any long entry produced by ANOTHER concept (FVG Reversal, Order Block Reversal, a candlestick reversal, etc.) only counts if it also falls within this discount zone at the moment of entry -- Premium/Discount adds no SL/TP logic of its own; the triggering concept's own SL/TP rules are used unchanged.

short_setup.title: Define the active range
short_setup.text: Same range as the long side.

short_setup.title: Calculate the premium zone
short_setup.text: The upper 50% of the range, mirrored from the discount calculation above.

short_setup.title: Require it as a filter, not a trigger
short_setup.text: Any short entry from another concept only counts if it also falls within the premium zone.

thresholds.note: Flagged as the clean, unambiguous default actually implemented (concepts.premium_discount_zone()), chosen deliberately over more complex Fibonacci-style subdivisions (e.g. a stricter 38.2%/61.8% band) -- those remain a valid future refinement, not built here.

detail.risk_note: Premium/Discount is a filter, not a signal. Using it alone, without a genuine entry trigger from another concept firing inside the correct zone, is not a valid trade -- it only ever narrows down WHERE another concept's setups are taken seriously, never fires a trade by itself.
detail.engine_note: This is a display/reference task only -- concepts.premium_discount_zone() already exists and is already wired into the engine's concept-column computation (concept name "premium_discount_zone", producing in_discount/in_premium columns), ready to be added as an extra AND-condition onto a future strategy's existing entry logic.
